checkedScope: Verified existence and metadata of all four citations: arXiv:2509.12337 (v2, 2026-03-23), arXiv:2504.20563, arXiv:2508.15878, and Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.17061968. Checked the specific content claims against the full text of 2509.12337 (abstract, Sec. 1, 3, 4.1-4.7, Tables 3-4) and the Coq-BB5 README. Did not check Appendix D (exact pipelines) or the detailed content of 2508.15878 beyond its abstract.
reasoning: All citations exist and are correctly attributed (authors, year, version, DOI). (1) arXiv:2509.12337 does prove S(5) = 47,176,870 in Coq by enumerating 181,385,789 machines in Tree Normal Form; its pipeline consists of Loops (cyclers and translated cyclers), NGramCPS, RepWL, FAR, WFAR and individual proofs for 13 Sporadic Machines, and it also proves S(2,4) = 3,932,964 (Theorem 1.2). (2) arXiv:2504.20563 explicitly presents deciders developed before the Coq proof that were mostly not used in it, so the distinction drawn between exploratory deciders and those in the final proof is accurate. (3) arXiv:2508.15878 synthesises Lean 4 theorem-proving challenges about Busy Beaver machines and halting bounds and does not claim a full Lean verification of BB(5); the description matches. (4) The Zenodo record is Coq-BB5 v1.0.0 by mxdys, containing BB(5), BB(2,4), BB(2), BB(3), BB(4) and BB(2,3) together with the enumerated machine lists. Table 4 of the paper confirms that the S(2,4) pipeline uses only Loops, NGramCPS and RepWL (plus simulation of long halters), so the recommendation to target BB(2,4) as an intermediate step, which needs no FAR/WFAR and no individual proofs, is well supported. The concluding statement that the cited literature does not establish a complete Lean port of Coq-BB5 or the equivalence of Coq and Lean implementations is appropriately cautious and correct with respect to the cited sources.
